title: Roman Law Treats Veneficium as Criminal Offense
description: By c. 353 BCE Roman law formally treated veneficium — encompassing both poisoning and magical harm — as a criminal offense subject to legal prosecution. The conflation of poison and magic in the Latin term veneficium is itself significant, reflecting the Roman conceptual difficulty in separating pharmacological from supernatural harm. This legal category will become foundational for later Roman magic legislation, particularly the Lex Cornelia of 81 BCE. The evidence for this date derives primarily from later compilations of Roman law, and some scholars treat it as the beginning of a legal tradition rather than a single datable event.
historiographical_note: John Scheid and Valerie Flint have examined veneficium as a conceptual category demonstrating the Roman conflation of poison and magic, foundational for later European legal traditions on harmful magic.
source_method: Published scholarship; Roman legal sources and secondary synthesis
